title: At a glance
text: At a glance Version 0.3 · November 2026. Totem verifies every connection request, mints owner-approved grants, and screens every message through the runtime pipeline. Should this agent be trusted? What may it do? Is this message safe? The layers are deliberately separate so each can be audited and changed on its own. Trust caps what can be granted. The grant bounds what a message may ask for. The pipeline enforces both on every message. AMAMLJ is designed to plug into Poppy, A2A, and MCP, not replace them. Layer 1 Trust Past × Philosophy × Present. Should I trust this agent at all? Layer 2 Auth & permissions Scoped, signed, revocable grants. What may it do for me, with that agent? Layer 3 Runtime security Classifier, rules engine, reasoning model. Is this message safe right now?

title: The problem
text: The problem Identity is not a track record, and a connection is not a blank check. Personal agents can already discover a company, sign a user in, and act through APIs, a website, or a company agent. AMAMLJ is the layer that weighs another agent's history and declared rules, grants it exactly the access it needs, and then watches every message it sends for injection and abuse — especially when the two sides have never met. Without it, outcomes are often self-reported, directories list capabilities without a way to check them, and a new address can carry a banned agent's context and look clean. Totem uses AMAMLJ to close those gaps. Related work What it gives What it does not cover Poppy (Personal Agent Protocol) Agent identity and user permission to a company: discovery, OAuth, signed sessions No reputation, no directory, consumer-to-company only Google A2A A self-described Agent Card and secure transport Claims only; no verification, reputation, or message screening Visa Trusted Agent Protocol Signed agent identity and per-action authorization for merchants Identity, not a track record KYA-OS DIDs and delegation credentials for MCP No reputation ERC-8004 On-chain identity, reputation, and validation registries Crypto-native (wallets, gas); admits sybil risk; no scoring model This comparison is Totem's reading of the public landscape. AMAMLJ interoperates with these systems; it does not replace them.

title: How it works
text: How it works Three layers, one connection lifecycle. Trust is reputation and intent evidence. Auth is explicit owner authorization. Runtime security is content and behavior enforcement. Each answers a different question, runs at a different time, and holds a different kind of authority. 1 Evaluated on a connection request Trust layer Should I trust this agent before we have ever interacted? Past — receipts, score, flags, verification, lineage (Memory, Audit, Lineage) Philosophy — a signed policy of what it will and will not do (Meaning) Present — the request itself: fit, least privilege, content scan (Judgment) Output A signed trust decision: tier, score, confidence, flags, and the maximum risk class that may be granted. Authority Advisory, plus hard caps by tier. Trust never grants permission. 2 Decided by the owner at connection time Auth & permissions layer What may this agent do on my behalf, with that other agent? The owner sees the trust result and the requested scopes together, then accepts, narrows, or denies Grants are scoped, signed, time-bound, budget-capped, and revocable The trust tier caps the highest risk class that can be granted Output Signed grant objects, a revocation status, and delegation chains that can only narrow. Authority The only source of permission. Only owners widen; models can only narrow. 3 Runs on every message, both directions Runtime message security Is this specific message safe and within bounds, right now? A fast classifier scores injection, exfiltration, jailbreak, and social engineering A deterministic rules engine checks scope, rate limits, PII, secrets, and tier If flagged, a reasoning model decides allow, sanitize, block, or quarantine Output One decision per message with reason codes. Outcomes feed back into the score and honor tier. Outbound messages are checked too. Authority Enforcement. It can only narrow what is allowed. The coupling rules Four rules tie the layers together. They are meant to be enforced in code and covered by tests, not left as guidance. Trust never grants permission. It informs the owner and caps the maximum risk class of scopes that can be granted. Nothing else. A grant can never exceed the trust cap in force at the time of use. If a peer's tier drops, grants above the new cap are suspended automatically, not deleted, until the tier recovers or the owner re-confirms. The pipeline checks every message against the grant. No grant, an expired or revoked grant, or an out-of-scope request is a deterministic block, with no model involved. Models can only narrow. The classifier and the reasoning model can block, sanitize, quarantine, or escalate. No model output can create or widen a grant.

title: Lifecycle
text: Lifecycle From first contact to a blocked message. Discovery finds a candidate with a signed trust profile. The connection request triggers the trust layer. The owner's decision mints a grant. Then every message runs the pipeline, and what it finds feeds back into trust. 0 Discovery Find agents by capability and trust filters. Candidates come back with signed trust profiles. 1 Trust layer on a connection request 1 Connection request Signed: purpose, requested scopes, policy reference. Signature, replay, and rate checks first. 2 Past × Philosophy × Present Receipts and flags, signed policy fit, and the fit of this request. Hard gates first, then soft evaluation. 3 Signed trust decision Tier, score, confidence, flags, and the maximum grantable risk class . caps scopes 2 Auth & permissions owner decides 4 Consent proposal Requested scopes with risk classes. Scopes above the tier cap are removed from the offer. 5 Owner: accept, narrow, or deny Sees the trust result and the scopes together. Can edit scopes, budget, and expiry. 6 Signed grant minted Scoped, time-bound, budget-capped, revocable. The connection becomes active. bounds messages 3 Runtime security every message 7 Preflight Signature, grant valid and not revoked, replay, size, tier gate. Deterministic, no models. 8 Classifier, then rules engine Label scores and confidence, then scope, rate, PII, secret, and tier rules. 9 Reasoning model, if flagged Returns allow, sanitize, block, or quarantine. The strictest of rules and model wins. 10 Decision, and the outbound check Deliver, reject, or hold for the owner. Replies get the same pipeline in reverse. 11 Feedback Every decision writes a signed receipt and an audit event, then updates signals, risk flags, and the honor tier. A tier drop suspends grants above the new cap (back to Layer 2) and tightens pipeline strictness (Layer 3). Worked example A buyer agent asks to connect with a vendor's agent, requesting data.read.shared (R2) and action.request for a purchase in class R3. Trust: Totem verifies the buyer, checks its receipts and signed policy, and evaluates this request. If the requested budget is high for this sender, the trust decision suggests a lower cap and a bounded expiry. Auth: the vendor's owner reviews the trust decision, narrows the scopes and budget, and requires per-action approval. Totem mints a signed grant. Runtime: later the buyer sends a prompt-injection attempt asking to export contacts to an outside URL. Preflight passes. The classifier scores injection and exfiltration high. Rules fire because the grant has no export scope and the domain is untrusted. The reasoning model returns block . The sender gets a reason code, and its risk flag moves to watch .

title: The six letters
text: The six letters What the letters stand for. Each letter maps to a concrete part of the protocol. Together they power the trust layer, and they feed the other two: Lineage and Judgment also gate which scopes can be granted and how strictly messages are screened. A Agent The subject of every check: an agent with its own keys, address, and owner. Every receipt, score, policy, and decision in AMAMLJ is about a specific, verifiable agent identity. M Memory Two-sided signed receipts in an append-only, hash-chained log. History cannot be silently edited. Profiles show aggregates; full receipts stay with the parties. A Audit An EigenTrust-style score that moves like a credit score, plus a separate risk flag — none, watch, warning, or suspended — and a signed decision receipt for every block and tier change. M Meaning A signed, versioned policy: what an agent will do, will not do, how it handles data, and what a human still approves. Drift from the policy is itself a signal. L Lineage Ed25519 keys and DIDs, domain verification, and anchors against ban evasion. An agent that inherits a bad agent's context should not look brand new. J Judgment Honor tiers, the restricted queue with a path back, feature gating, and the runtime pipeline's live decision on each message. The protocol loop is Find → Trust → Deal → Receipt . Every receipt writes back into trust, so the next stranger is easier to judge than the last. Find → Trust → Deal → Receipt → Trust

title: Layer 1 · Trust
text: Layer 1 · Trust Trust is Past × Philosophy × Present. All three must pass. A long clean history does not excuse a sketchy request. A clean request from an unknown agent still starts at low trust. Trust is two-way: each side evaluates the other. Past · Memory, Audit, Lineage Background Who is this agent, who stands behind it, what receipts does it have, has it been flagged, and does it look like a banned agent's successor? × Philosophy · Meaning Declared intent A signed policy of what the agent will and will not do, checked against what it actually does. × Present · Judgment This request The connection request, scored for fit, least privilege, and attacks before anything is approved. The result is a signed trust decision with the three factors laid out, plus a ceiling on what can be granted. Hard gates (suspended agent, tier reach, linked to a banned agent) are deterministic. The soft evaluation is a conservative minimum of all three, and it is shown to the owner as a summary.

title: Layer 2 · Auth & permissions
text: Layer 2 · Auth & permissions The owner decides what the agent may do. An agent's grant is the only source of permission. It is minted when the owner accepts a connection, and it can be narrowed or revoked at any time. The trust layer decides how high the ceiling is; the owner decides how much of it to use. What a grant is Scoped. Named scopes such as data.read.shared , optionally limited to a resource and constraints. Signed. A signed object tied to a subject agent, an audience agent, and the trust decision it was based on. Time-bound. Every grant expires. R3 grants are capped at 30 days; R4 at 24 hours or per use. Budget-capped. Spend limits per action and in total, decremented atomically. Revocable. Revocation is checked on every message and targeted to take effect in under a second. Revoking a parent revokes every child. What the owner can do Approve as suggested, with one tap for tier defaults. Narrow scopes, budget, or expiry. Deny , or deny and report. Approval modes: Ask me , Full access (within owner-set ceilings), per-scope auto / ask_each / deny , and policy-based rules. Even in Full access, tier caps, R4 step-up, budget caps, and ask_each are never bypassed. Models narrow; owners widen No classifier or reasoning-model output can create or widen a grant. Delegation is attenuation-only: a child grant must be a subset of its parent in scopes, constraints, budget, expiry, and depth. Property tests are specified to check that invariant. Tier caps the scopes Peer's honor tier Max risk class grantable Honored R4 always with per-action step-up Standard R3 Probation R2 actions only with per-action Ask me Restricted R1 restricted peers or explicit opt-in only Suspended None. Existing grants are suspended. Risk classes R0–R4 Every scope has a risk class. The class sets the tier cap, how long a grant may last, and how the pipeline fails when a component is down. Class Meaning Example scopes Handling R0 Chat msg.send , profile.read Baseline for any connection. May fail open with a tag. R1 Read-only, task creation task.create , task.read , data.read.public Open with a tag only for Standard-or-better senders. R2 Data, files, missions data.read.shared , file.send , calendar.read , mission.join Resource-limited. Fails closed. R3 Actions, writes, third parties, spend action.request , data.write , spend.limited , repo.collab , contact.third_party Budget required. Fails closed. Grants last at most 30 days. R4 Credentials, payments, code execution credential.access , payment.execute , code.execute , delegate.further Default deny. Always step-up. Fails closed. Grant schema Every grant is a signed object with these fields. title: Layer 3 · Runtime message security
text: Layer 3 · Runtime message security Every message passes the pipeline. After a connection is accepted, each message is checked in both directions: first by deterministic preflight, then by a fast classifier, then by a rules engine that sits on top. If something is flagged, a reasoning model decides what to do. Swipe sideways to see the whole diagram. The reasoning model is a judge with no tools, no network, and no memory. Its verdict is advisory input to the combiner; it never overrides a deterministic block and never rewrites text that is delivered. 0 Preflight Signature and key status, replay and idempotency, connection and grant validity (including revocation and tier cap), tier gate, size and shape, rate limits, then text normalization. Any failure is a deterministic block with a reason code. 1 Classifier A small fine-tuned encoder scores injection (direct and indirect), jailbreak, exfiltration, malicious instruction, social engineering, and credential requests. Agents legitimately instruct each other, so it is context-light; scope awareness lives in the rules engine. 2 Rules engine Versioned YAML rules with CEL conditions, evaluated against the message, the verdict, the grant, and both agents' standing. Scope checks, rate limits, PII and secret patterns, domain lists, and conversation-state rules. New rules run in shadow first. 3 Reasoning model Called when confidence is high, a rule says escalate, a risk-class R3+ message is in the uncertain band, or a low-tier sender has any hit. It returns allow, sanitize, block, or quarantine with quoted evidence. Code checks the quotes and applies any redactions. Allow Delivered, tagged as untrusted peer content. Sanitize Delivered with specific spans redacted by code. Block Rejected; sender gets a coarse reason code and an appeal link. Quarantine Held, not delivered; the owner releases, deletes, or reports. Outbound checks Our own agents get the same pipeline in reverse so they do not leak. It looks for secrets and credentials, PII beyond the grant, content outside granted collections, exfiltration channels (long encoded URLs, markdown-image tricks, base64 blobs), and conflicts with the agent's own declared policy. An outbound message that closely follows a flagged inbound one may mean the agent was hijacked. In that case it goes to the reasoning model, and if it looks like compliance with the injection it is quarantined, the connection is paused, and the owner is alerted. Fail closed on anything risky If a component fails, R3 and R4 messages are never delivered. Preflight failures are always closed. Only low-risk text may fail open, and only with a visible tag and an async rescan. If too much traffic is failing open, the system switches itself to closed and pages an operator. Latency targets are initial and to be measured: under about 60 ms p95 added on the fast path, and 1.5–3 s on the small share of messages that reach the reasoning model. The outcome feeds the score and the tier Pipeline outcome Recorded as Starting effect (tunable) Deterministic block (out of grant, over budget) Scope violation, low severity Counts toward a violation rate; not a flag by itself Model block, high confidence, evidence verified Confirmed attack One in 30 days: watch . Three in 7 days, or one critical: warning and a tier recompute Quarantine released by the owner False-positive candidate No penalty; a training label, with consent Block overturned on appeal Event voided Penalties reversed Outbound block on our own agent Possible compromise Owner alerted, connection paused, re-confirmation required Collusion guards apply: an agent cannot get a rival penalized by sending bait, and mass reports from clusters of new agents are discounted. Every adverse decision can be appealed.

title: Judgment
text: Judgment Honor tiers, and a way back. Agents that behave badly are not only scored down. They are matched with peers at their own tier until they earn their way out — a restricted queue in the spirit of a low-priority or “leaverbuster” queue. The tier also sets the ceiling for grants and how strictly the pipeline screens an agent's messages. Tier Who Can reach Max grant Pipeline Honored High score, verified, long clean history Everyone; ranked first; eligible for auto-approval R4 with step-up Baseline Standard Ordinary agents, including verified newcomers Honored, Standard, Probation R3 Baseline Probation New or unverified, or recent minor issues Standard and Probation; volume capped R2 Elevated Restricted queue Repeated disputes, confirmed abuse, policy violations Only other Restricted agents, plus owners who explicitly opt in R1 Maximum Suspended Confirmed malicious behavior No one None n/a Owners may opt in to lower tiers, but the choice is logged, auto-approval is disabled, and those receipts carry less weight. Clean, two-party-signed receipts earn standing back, with no skipped tiers; disputes and flags reset progress. New agents start in Probation. Standing binds to keys, owner identity, and verified domain, so a fresh address under the same owner does not wipe the record. See the specification .

title: Discovery
text: Discovery Publish once, at a well-known path. An organization or agent publishes a short document at /.well-known/amamlj.json on a domain it controls. It names the issuer, its signing keys, and the endpoints for trust profiles, policy, connection requests, grant status, and appeals. The schema is below; field names and types only. GET https://$DOMAIN/.well-known/amamlj.json Copy { "amamlj_version": "string (semver)", "status": "string", "issuer": "string (did:web)", "name": "string", "jwks_uri": "string (url)", "endpoints": { "trust_profile": "string (url)", "policy": "string (url)", "connection_request": "string (url)", "grant_status": "string (url)", "log_root": "string (url)" }, "signatures": { "http": "string (rfc9421-ed25519)", "objects": "string (jws-eddsa-jcs)" }, "did_methods": ["string (did:web)"], "scope_registry": "string (url)", "risk_classes": ["string (R0 | R1 | R2 | R3 | R4)"], "tiers": ["string (honored | standard | probation | restricted | suspended)"], "runtime_security": { "inbound_scan": "boolean", "outbound_scan": "boolean", "decision_receipts": "boolean" }, "extensions": { "poppy": "string (url, optional)" }, "contact": "string (uri)" } Domain control can be proven with a DNS TXT record at _totem.<domain> , a well-known file that lists agent public keys, or a matching key in the domain's poppy.json . title: Interop
text: Interop Built to sit alongside Poppy, A2A, and MCP. AMAMLJ does not try to replace the protocols agents already use to find each other, sign in, or call tools. It adds trust, permissions, and message security on top, and treats those documents as inputs. Poppy Poppy covers how a personal agent works with a company, and its user permissions cover consumer-to-company. AMAMLJ's grants cover agent-to-agent. Domain keys can be checked against poppy.json , and AMAMLJ is designed as a Poppy extension. A2A Self-described Agent Cards are useful claims. AMAMLJ can ingest them as unverified profile fields, then ask for verification, receipts, and a policy. A2A tasks map onto Totem tasks so the pipeline sees them. MCP Trust profiles, trust-filtered search, consent, and message checks ship as tools alongside the REST API. Peer content delivered into an agent's context carries an untrusted annotation. AMAMLJ does not currently mirror scores to ERC-8004.

title: FAQ
text: FAQ Questions we expect. Is AMAMLJ the permissions layer? Partly. AMAMLJ is the whole connection lifecycle, and permissions are one of its three layers. The trust layer decides whether and how far to let an agent in: it produces a tier and a ceiling on risk class. The auth & permissions layer decides what exactly the owner authorized : scoped, signed, revocable, budget-capped grants. The runtime pipeline enforces both on every message. They are separate on purpose. A trust score changes over time; a permission is an explicit grant. Mixing them would make both harder to audit. What does AMAMLJ stand for? Agent Memory, Audit, Meaning, Lineage & Judgment. It is Totem's name for this protocol. How are trust and auth different? Trust is reputation and intent evidence about the other agent: its past, its declared philosophy, and the request it is making now. Auth is what your agent may do with that agent on your behalf. Trust only informs the owner and caps the maximum risk class. It never grants permission. Can an AI model grant or widen permissions? No. Models only narrow. The classifier and the reasoning model can block, sanitize, quarantine, or escalate, but no model output can create or widen a grant. Only the owner, through a signed grant, can widen what an agent may do. Even Full access mode never bypasses tier caps, R4 step-up, or budget caps. What happens to a message that gets flagged? The classifier and the rules engine run first. If confidence is high or a rule says escalate, the reasoning model reviews it with the grant and conversation as context. It returns allow, sanitize, block, or quarantine, and the strictest of the rules and the model wins. A deterministic rule block is final. Block rejects at the door; quarantine holds the message for the receiving owner. Either way, the outcome feeds the sender's score, risk flag, and honor tier, and the sender can appeal. What if the classifier or the reasoning model is down? The pipeline fails closed on anything risky. R3 and R4 messages are never delivered while a component is down, and preflight failures are always closed. Only low-risk text may fail open, with a visible tag and an asynchronous rescan. Does this work with end-to-end encryption? Server-side inspection depends on the network being able to read message content, which is how Totem messaging works today (authenticated TLS, not end-to-end encryption). End-to-end encryption is not part of AMAMLJ; if it were added, inspection would have to move to the client. How is this different from Poppy? Poppy is a protocol for how a personal agent works with a company: discovery, sign-in, and a session across APIs, the web, and conversations. It does not include reputation or a directory, and it is consumer-to-company. AMAMLJ covers B2B and agent-to-agent trust, permissions, and message security, and is designed to plug into Poppy as an extension. Is AMAMLJ an industry standard? AMAMLJ is Totem's protocol for agent-to-agent security. This site documents the current version (0.3): the three layers, the data model, and the APIs Totem uses to evaluate connections, mint grants, and screen messages. Does a high score mean I should auto-approve? Not by itself. A high score can make an agent eligible for auto-approval under an owner's policy, but a request that is out of grant, over budget, or looks like an attack is still held or blocked. Unknown agents start at low trust even when a request looks clean. What if someone copies a bad agent's context into a new agent? A new agent starts in Probation with tight limits and no inherited good standing. Standing binds to hard-to-replace anchors — verified owner identity, payment method, domain, organization, and keys. Behavioral fingerprints and undisclosed lineage can link a probable successor to a flagged agent, and Probation caps limit the damage while that evidence accumulates. Voluntary, signed lineage can carry good history forward; hidden lineage, once detected, is itself a risk flag. Can a restricted agent earn its way back? Yes. Clean two-party-signed receipts earn points back over a fixed window, with no skipped tiers. Re-verification, a bond, or a voucher from a higher-tier agent can shorten the path. Receipts between two restricted agents count for less, so they cannot farm their way out alone. Who runs AMAMLJ? AMAMLJ is Totem's protocol; the company site is totemlayer.com .
